build: PAL cassette, Pandora 1987, analysed at the loader's hand-over

exclude: runtime: the screen, which the game fills with tiles and the status panel; the bytes the loader left here are its own loading screen
runtime: the sprite pointers and the bytes beside them, written at the start of every mission
runtime: the figures' positions on the floor, filled in by the map builder at $6A40 as it reads the floor's description
runtime: the figures' places in the castle map and their kinds, filled in by the map builder
runtime: the 256 random bytes $67CA reads out of the sound chip's noise oscillator at start-up
runtime: the buffer the message printer at $5935 fills with the characters of the line being shown
runtime: untouched at the hand-over, inside the map builder's working area
runtime: the top quarter of the castle map, built from the floor's description by $6A40
runtime: the bottom part of the castle map, built from the floor's description by $6A40
extra: the title picture's bitmap, loaded from tape and shown while the rest of the tape loads; the castle map is built over it once the game runs

comments.text: which floor the player is on, 0 the basement to 3 the second floor
how many rows of blocks of the floor are still to be built
the message line's fine horizontal scroll, stepped down by 4 each frame; when it wraps the text is shifted a character along
what the player walked off the edge of: the bits say which way, and the room builder reads it to bring the next room in
how many door keys the player is carrying, in binary-coded decimal; the panel prints it
which of the player's two shots are in the air: bit 0 the first, bit 4 the second. Bit 1 is flipped when the first shot turns back at a room edge and bit 5 likewise for the second.
the way the player is facing, which is the way a shot goes: 1 up, 2 down, 3 left, 4 right
the way the first shot is travelling, 1 up, 2 down, 3 left, 4 right, taken from the player's facing when it was fired
how far the first shot has travelled, in pixels; the second shot cannot be fired until this has passed 8
the way the second shot is travelling
how far the second shot has travelled
set while fire is still held, so one press fires one shot
the position across the room a tile lookup is about, in pixels
the position down the room a tile lookup is about, in pixels
counts frames 0 to 3; the player may move on the frame it reaches 3, so one step takes four frames
the screen code of the upper digit $5A20 has just made
the screen code of the lower digit $5A20 has just made
how many rounds the player has, kept in binary-coded decimal so the panel can print it a digit at a time. A mission starts with $99, that is 99.
counts the frames the player has not moved; the nag "COME ON ! GET ON WITH IT....." waits on it
the top two digits of the score, in binary-coded decimal
the middle two digits of the score
the bottom two digits of the score
points waiting to be added to the score, in binary-coded decimal; the panel's own routine takes them a digit at a time
how many hits the player has taken, in binary-coded decimal. Cold food takes $10 off it, first aid clears it, and the panel prints it.
2 when the player is dead, which ends the game
set while the game is paused, so the interrupt leaves the game alone and only keeps the message line going
where the player is in the castle, across, counted in tiles: the position in the room plus the room's own offset
where the player is in the castle, down, counted in tiles
how many figures the floor's description put on this floor
which column of blocks the builder is filling in
which row of blocks the builder is filling in
the direction the shot that just hit something was travelling, kept so the thing hit knows which way the bullet came
$FF once the mission's job is done, which the main loop watches for
which sound to start, read once a frame by $63F3: 1 to 9, and 0 for none. Firing sets 5, a shot that hits something useless 2, a mirror 3, healing 4, a pickup 9 and a hit on a figure 1.
which sound effect is in progress, so the tick at $6615 can carry it on
how many frames the sound in progress has left
which of the two walking shapes the player is drawn with, taken from the lowest bit of the step count
flips with the player's step so the footsteps alternate between two pitches
counts the player's steps; its lowest bit is the walking frame $02D8
the first shot's position across the room, in pixels
the first shot's position down the room, in pixels
the second shot's position across the room, in pixels
the second shot's position down the room, in pixels
the player's position across the room, in pixels, which the four player sprites are placed from
the player's position down the room, in pixels
how far through the table of random numbers the game has got; it runs round and round the 256 bytes
set while the player's shot is in the air, so the turn waits for fire to be let go before anything else happens
the floor the player was on before the lift, kept so the game can tell whether the prisoner was left behind
what the game's own code wants the main loop to do next: 1 the lift, 2 a prisoner delivered home
the low byte of the lift's place in the castle map
the high byte of the lift's place in the castle map
where in the castle map the prisoner is, low byte
where in the castle map the prisoner is, high byte
which of the three phases of the interrupt's rota comes next, so the heavy work is spread over three frames
jump stub into the high score check at $0B89, called from the game's own code at $4943 and $4AA3 when a game ends
the player's score as six ASCII digits, "000000" at the hand-over; read when the score is drawn and when a high score is checked
the name being typed, ten ASCII characters, all "." at the hand-over, which the name-entry screen fills in and the high score table takes
the colour the attract and high score screens draw their text in; read and written by the screen builders at $0B89 and $0CF9
jump stub into the death screen at $1A21, called from the game at $4931
jump stub into the floor-select screen at $1AB2, called from the game at $499E when the player rides the lift
jump stub into the mission-select screen at $1D23, called from the game at $4966
jump stub into the mission briefing at $1E3F, called from the game at $4A4E
which mission the player chose, 1 to 4, set by the mission-select screen and read by the briefing and the end-of-mission screens
jump stub into the end-of-mission screen at $1F3C, called from the game at $4AA0

stops CIA 1's timer A, turns the video chip's raster interrupt on, points the interrupt vector $0314 at the handler at $085A, asks for the first interrupt on line 0 and clears the band counter at $0859. Called once, from $0CD9.
which band of the attract screen's raster split the next interrupt serves, 0 to 3; the handler at $085A steps it and wraps it to 0

the attract screens' raster interrupt, a chain of four bands counted by $0859. Band 0 sets the picture at the top ($08A5) and asks for line $78, band 1 the text below it ($08FC) and line $C6, band 2 the scrolling strip's fine position ($0929) and line $DA, band 3 puts the fine position back ($0935) and line 0. Band 0 ends by jumping into the KERNAL's own interrupt handler at $EA31, so the jiffy clock and the keyboard still run; the other three return with RTI.

band 0: multicolour bitmap mode ($D011 = $3B, $D016 = $D8) with video bank 3, so the plaque's bitmap at $E000 and its colours at $EC00 are what the top of the screen shows. Then reads the joystick ($0A13) and redraws the name-entry cursor ($0940).
switches to multicolour text with the screen at $0400 and the character set at $2800, video bank 0, blanking the display for the change ($D011 = $7B, then $1B). Called from $0FB2.

band 1: single-colour text with the screen at $0400 and the character set at $2800, video bank 0, so the words below the picture are drawn from the two-cell-wide alphabet. Blanks the display across the change, as $08D0 does.
the fine horizontal position of the name-entry screen's scrolling alphabet, 0 to 7 in the video chip's own units; band 2 puts it into $D016 and the joystick routine steps it by 4
band 2: puts $0928 into the low four bits of $D016, which scrolls the alphabet strip at the bottom of the name-entry screen sideways without redrawing it
band 3: puts the fine horizontal position back to 0 and 40 columns ($D016 low nibble = 8), so only the strip's own band is scrolled
draws the character the name-entry strip has under its cursor at row 23, column 10 plus twice the letter's place, taking the character from the strip position $070B and the cursor from $0CD3
set when the name-entry screen has acted on a stick push, cleared when the stick comes back to the middle, so one push moves the cursor one place

what fire does on the name-entry screen: takes the character the strip shows, and either steps the cursor on (up to ten characters) or, when the strip shows the end mark, draws a full stop and steps the cursor back one. Called from the joystick reader at $0A13.
how far the name-entry alphabet strip has scrolled, in half-characters, 0 to $5F; $09AB redraws the strip from it and the joystick steps it
the strip position in whole characters, $09A9 shifted right; $09AB indexes the alphabet at $0B48 with it

redraws the name-entry screen's alphabet strip into rows 23 and 24 from the alphabet at $0B48, starting at the character $09A9 names and wrapping at the 48th. On an even half-step it writes each character's four cells in place; on an odd one it writes the right-hand half of one character beside the left-hand half of the next, which is how the strip moves half a character at a time.

reads the joystick on control port 2 ($DC00) for the name-entry screen: left scrolls the alphabet strip one way ($0A37), right the other ($0A5A), fire takes the character under the cursor ($095E), and the middle position clears the one-push-at-a-time flag $095D. Called once a frame from band 0 of the attract interrupt.

scrolls the name-entry alphabet strip one step right: adds 4 to the fine position, and when that reaches 8 puts it back to 0 and moves the strip back a half-character, wrapping at $5F, then redraws the strip

scrolls the name-entry alphabet strip one step left: takes 4 from the fine position, and when that underflows puts it back to 4 and moves the strip on a half-character, wrapping at $60, then redraws the strip
the top-left cell's code, worked out by the plotter at $0A84
the top-right cell's code
the bottom-left cell's code
the bottom-right cell's code
the character the plotter at $0A84 is to draw, already masked to six bits (so A is 1 and the digit 0 is $30)
the column the plotter writes at, 0 to 39, stepped on by 2 after each character
the row the plotter writes at, stepped on by 2 when the column passes 39
the colour the plotter puts in both of the character's upper colour cells
the colour for both of its lower cells

draws one character of the big alphabet, which is two cells wide and two high. Multiplies $0A7F by four for the four cell codes (top-left n, bottom-left n+1, top-right n+2, bottom-right n+3), builds the screen address $0400 + 40 * $0A81 + $0A80 by adding 40 a row at a time, writes the four codes, adds $D4 to the pointer's high byte to reach colour memory at $D800 and writes $0A82 to the upper pair and $0A83 to the lower, then steps the column on by two and the row by two when the column passes 39. 48 places call it.
"     WELL DONE      YOU ARE A REAL HERO ", ASCII ending $FF; drawn as two rows of twenty characters by $0C28
"  ENTER YOUR NAME", ASCII ending $FF

the 48 characters the name-entry strip offers, ASCII ending $FF: "@ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ 0123456789!\"#$%&'()_" and a run of full stops. $09AB draws it and wraps at the 48th, so the strip is endless.

compares the score at $0819, digit by digit as ASCII, with each of the ten entries in the table at $0D51, twenty bytes apart. On the first entry the score beats, it goes to the name entry at $0BC1; on an equal entry it compares the next digit; otherwise it steps $0829 on by 20 and tries the next, and when that passes $C8 the score made no entry and it returns to the attract loop at $1014. Blanks the display and banks every ROM in on the way in.

builds the name-entry screen. Steps $0829 back to the entry the score beat, copies the colour memory of the plaque at the top from the tables at $EE00 and $EF00 with the KERNAL banked out, clears the rows below with the big alphabet's space, puts the strip at character $4F, sets the colour of the three regions the screen uses, and draws the strip and the two lines of text. It then installs the attract interrupt at $0CD9 and waits for ten characters.

draws the two lines of the name-entry screen, "WELL DONE / YOU ARE A REAL HERO" from $0B0D and "ENTER YOUR NAME" from $0B36, each ending $FF, through the plotter at $0A84, and then the end mark the strip uses. Each line has its own pair of colours, and after twenty characters of the first line it drops a row.
how many characters of the name have been typed, 0 to 10; the name-entry screen waits for it to reach 10, and fire steps it
spins until ten characters have been typed, with the attract interrupt doing the work: the strip, the cursor and the joystick are all handled by band 0
reads the ten typed characters back off the screen itself, from row 23 at $07A3 taking every other cell, shifts each right twice to undo the plotter's multiply by four, and leaves them in $081F

makes room for the new entry by copying the table down twenty bytes, from the end back to the place the score beat, then fills the entry with spaces, the name from $081F and the score from $0819. The source address $0D3C is simply $0D51 less twenty; the bytes there are a delay loop, not a table.

a two-deep delay loop that holds the finished high score table on a blank screen before the attract loop starts again at $1014. The shift at $0CF8 reads these same bytes as its source, which is only how it addresses the table twenty bytes lower.
ten high score entries of 20 bytes: a seven-character name, padding, and a six-digit score, all ASCII
the high score table's heading, "TODAYS REAL HEROES" with the spaces that centre it, ASCII ending $FF

installs the title screen's fade interrupt: blanks the display, black border and background, stops CIA 1's timer A, points $0314 at $0E6A, asks for line 0 and turns the raster interrupt on. Called from the title screen builder at $1024.

the title screen's raster interrupt: a fade worked by rewriting colour memory. $1012 says which phase it is in (0 fade in, 2 fade out, 3 hold, 1 and 4 idle), $1011 the step inside it, 0 to 9. Each step takes four colours from the tables at $0FE5, $0FEF, $0FF9 and $1003, puts them in $100D to $1010 and calls $0EF9 to paint the four bands of the screen with them. The fade in counts up to 10 and goes to the hold, the hold counts $1013 to 256 and starts the fade out, the fade out counts down to 0 and stops. It then calls the music at $1947 and ends through the KERNAL's handler at $EA31.
writes the four colours in $100D to $1010 into the four bands of colour memory the title screen uses, forty cells each, so one call recolours the whole picture. Called by both halves of the fade.

installs the interrupt the credits, supplies and valuables screens run on. Banks every ROM in, blanks the display, copies the plaque's colour memory from $EE00 and $EF00 with the KERNAL banked out, stops CIA 1's timer A, clears the band flag $0F94, points $0314 at $0F95 and asks for line 0. Called from $11C8.
which of the two bands the plaque screens' interrupt serves next, flipped each time: 0 draws the picture at the top, 1 the text below it

the interrupt the credits, supplies and valuables screens run on, two bands flipped by $0F94. On the picture band it switches to the bitmap ($0FC0), asks for line $78 and plays the music at $1947, ending through the KERNAL's handler at $EA31; on the text band it switches back to text ($08D0), asks for line 0 and returns with RTI.
switches the top of the screen to the multicolour bitmap of the stone plaque: bitmap mode, white background 0, video bank 3 and $D018 = $B8, so the bitmap is at $E000 and its colours at $EC00
the first band's colour for each of the ten fade steps
the second band's colour for each step
the third band's colour for each step
the fourth band's colour for each step
the colour the fade's current step gives the first band of the title screen
the second band's colour for this step
the third band's colour for this step
the fourth band's colour for this step
which of the ten steps of the title screen's fade is showing, an index into the four colour tables at $0FE5
which phase the title screen's fade is in: 0 fades in, 2 fades out, 3 holds the picture, 1 and 4 leave it alone
counts the frames the finished title picture is held, from 0 round to 0 again, which is 256 frames, about five seconds on a PAL machine

builds the title screen. Starts the music at $18D6, sets the fade to its first phase, installs the fade interrupt at $0E40, selects video bank 0 with the screen at $0400 and the character set at $2800 in single-colour text, fills all four pages of the screen with the big alphabet's space, then draws the heading at $0E2C and the whole high score table at $0D50, two hundred characters, through the plotter at $0A84. It ends in the wait at $10AF.
waits on the title screen: fire on control port 2 goes to the mission select at $1566, and when the fade reaches its last phase ($1012 = 4) the attract loop moves on to the credits screen at $11AB
"  PROGRAMMING BY", ASCII ending $FF
"  ANDREW CHALLIS", ASCII ending $FF
"    GRAPHICS BY", ASCII ending $FF
"   ROBIN CHAPMAN", ASCII ending $FF
five spaces, drawn before "VALUABLES" so the heading sits centred
the valuables screen's heading and its four items, ASCII, each ending $00
"PAINTING", ASCII ending $00
"VASE", ASCII ending $00
"PENDANT", ASCII ending $00
"GEMSTONES", ASCII ending $00

draws the four-cell-wide, thirteen-row block of character $E8 down the left of the supplies and valuables screens, which is the frame the four item pictures sit in, taking its colour from the byte at $8600. Walks the screen and colour memory together, adding 40 a row.
the supplies screen's heading and its four items, ASCII, each ending $00
" SUPPLIES ", ASCII ending $00
"COLD FOOD", ASCII ending $00
"DOOR KEY", ASCII ending $00
"AMMUNITION", ASCII ending $00
"FIRST AID", ASCII ending $00

builds the credits screen: fills the screen with the big alphabet's space, sets the two extra background colours the plaque's bitmap needs, installs the plaque interrupt at $0F4D, and draws the four credit lines from $10C8, $10D9, $10EA and $10FA

holds the credits screen for about three seconds, polling fire on control port 2 all the way through so a press goes straight to the mission select at $1566. When nothing is pressed it builds the valuables screen.

copies the pictures of the four valuables out of the play screen's character set at $2000 into the top sixteen codes of the attract screen's set at $2F40, so the icons beside PAINTING, VASE, PENDANT and GEMSTONES are the very tiles the player picks up in the castle. Four cells each, taken from $2000, $20A0, $20C0, $2140 and $2330.

builds the valuables screen: clears it to the big alphabet's space, draws the icon frames at $113A, puts the four icons' cell codes in place, and then draws the heading and the four names through the plotter

puts the cell codes of the four valuables' pictures on the valuables screen, two by two, and takes each one's colour from the tile colour table at $8600, the same table the castle's rooms are coloured from
draws the valuables screen's heading and the four names, PAINTING, VASE, PENDANT and GEMSTONES, each from its own string and at its own row, through the plotter at $0A84
holds the valuables screen for about three seconds, polling fire all the way through so a press goes to the mission select at $1566, then builds the supplies screen

copies the pictures of the four supplies out of the play screen's character set at $2000 into the top codes of the attract screen's set at $2F80, from $20E0, $2100, $2080, $2090 and $2000, so the icons beside COLD FOOD, DOOR KEY, AMMUNITION and FIRST AID are the tiles the player picks up
builds the supplies screen: draws the icon frames at $113A, places the four icons' cell codes with their colours from the tile colour table at $8600, and draws the heading and the four names
draws the supplies screen's heading " SUPPLIES " and the four names, COLD FOOD, DOOR KEY, AMMUNITION and FIRST AID, each at its own row, through the plotter at $0A84

holds the supplies screen for about three seconds, polling fire all the way through so a press goes to the mission select at $1566. With nothing pressed the attract loop starts again at $1017, which rebuilds the title screen without restarting the music.

leaves the attract loop for the game. Blanks the screen, clears all four pages of colour memory, keeps video bank 0 but points $D018 at $15, so the screen stays at $0400 and the characters come from the machine's own character ROM at $1000 - which is why the mission select is the only screen in the game written in the C64's own font. Turns the raster interrupt off, starts CIA 1's timer A and puts the KERNAL's own handler back in $0314, banks every ROM in, silences all 25 sound registers, waits for fire to be let go, and jumps into the game at $4000.
voice 1's tune, one note number a step, read by the driver at $1947; $FF ends it and starts all three voices again
voice 2's tune, one note number a step
voice 3's tune, one note number a step
the frequency high byte of each note the tune uses, indexed by note number
the frequency low byte of each note, indexed by note number
how many driver ticks each note lasts, indexed by note number
starts the music: clears the three voices' counters and stream positions, sets the SID's volume to 15, and leaves the driver at $1947 to do the rest a frame at a time
the waveform and gate each voice plays with: $41 pulse for voices 1 and 3, $21 sawtooth for voice 2. The driver clears bit 0 to let a note go and writes the byte again to start the next.
how many driver ticks are left of each voice's current note, one byte a voice; when it reaches zero the voice takes its next note
how far each voice has read into its own stream, one byte a voice
the frequency high byte each voice is playing, one byte a voice
the frequency low byte each voice is playing, one byte a voice
which of the three voices the driver is serving, 0 to 2
the offset of that voice's registers from $D400: 0, 7 or 14
the note number each voice has just taken from its stream, one byte a voice; $FF ends the tune
counts frames 0, 1, 2 so the driver only acts on every third one

the music, one tick at a time, called once a frame from the title and plaque interrupts. It does nothing on two frames in three, so the tune runs at about 16.7 ticks a second on a PAL machine. On the third it serves each of the three voices in turn: it counts the voice's note down, and when that runs out takes the next note number from the voice's own stream ($15E2, $1680 or $1768), looks the number up in the three note tables to get the frequency high byte, the low byte and the length, writes the frequency and the waveform to that voice, and steps the stream on. A note number of $FF ends the tune, and the driver starts all three streams again from the beginning, so the music is endless.
"YOU ARE DEAD", ASCII ending $00
clears colour memory, puts the screen back to the big alphabet's character set at $2800 in single-colour text, and draws "YOU ARE DEAD" across the middle
"SELECT FLOOR", ASCII ending $00

the four floors the lift serves, thirteen characters each and a $00: BASEMENT, GROUND FLOOR, FIRST FLOOR, SECOND FLOOR. The floor-select screen draws them as a list, and the message line names the same four at $5808.
which floor the lift's list has the marker against, 0 to 3, counting up from the basement

builds the screen the lift shows: blanks the display, clears colour memory, sets multicolour text from the character set at $2800 with the two extra background colours the list needs, and draws "SELECT FLOOR" and the four floor names, each in its own colours

the floor-select screen's own loop. It marks the floor the player is on to begin with, taken from $02A7, then waits: up and down move the marker, wrapping round the four floors, and each move rubs out the old marker and draws the new one at column 32 of the floor's row. Fire returns the chosen floor in A. Between repeats it idles for about a fiftieth of a second and then waits for raster line $F0, so the marker steps at a readable pace.
the pause between two steps of the floor marker: a counted loop and then a wait for raster line $F0, which is what stops one push running through all four floors
"SELECT MISSION", ASCII ending $00
builds the mission-select screen - clears colour memory, single-colour text from the character set at $2800 - draws "SELECT MISSION" and the number, and then waits in $1D99

the mission-select screen's loop: up steps the mission number on, down steps it back, each wrapping round 1 to 4 and redrawing the digit, and fire shows the briefing at $1E3F and returns the chosen mission in A. Between steps it idles about a quarter of a second.
draws the mission number at row 10, column 18. The digit shown is five minus $0836, so the number on the screen counts the other way from the number the game keeps: the screen's 1 is $0836 = 4.
steps $0836 on by one, wrapping from 4 back to 1, and redraws the digit
steps $0836 back by one, wrapping from 1 round to 4, and redraws the digit
"MISSION", the heading of the mission briefing
the second line of the briefing's heading, ASCII ending $00
"RESCUE THE PRISONER"
"BLOW UP THE CASTLE"

the briefing the mission select shows when fire is pressed: clears the screen, draws "MISSION", the number and then one of the two orders - "BLOW UP THE CASTLE" when $0836 is 4, "RESCUE THE PRISONER" otherwise - and holds it for about three seconds. Because the digit drawn is five minus $0836, the screen that reads MISSION 1 is the one that orders the castle blown up.
holds the finished briefing on screen for about three seconds before play begins
"WELL DONE !"
"YOUR MISSION WAS A" and, after it, "SUCCESS"

the screen that follows a mission the player finished: blanks the display, puts the screen back on the big alphabet's character set at $2800 in single-colour text, clears colour memory and draws "WELL DONE !", "YOUR MISSION WAS A" and "SUCCESS", each in its own place

the play screen's character set, 256 tiles of eight bytes. It holds the castle's walls, floors, doors, furniture, the figures, the pickups, the status panel's frame, the ten letters the panel needs and the digits at $F0 to $F9. facts.md has the letters' codes.
the upper half of the play screen's character set, tiles $80 to $FF, which hold the panel's frame and the digits

the character set the attract screens and the message line are written in. Each character of text is a block of two cells by two, so one letter takes four of these, and the code of its first cell is the ASCII value masked to six bits and multiplied by four.
the upper half of the big alphabet, which holds the digits, the punctuation and the sixteen cells the attract screens borrow for the item pictures at $2F40

the sprite shapes, 64 bytes each, which the pointers at $07F8 name as a number from $C0. The player's four are $C0 to $C3, and $E0 to $EF are the four he is drawn with for each of the four directions.
more sprite shapes, numbers $D0 to $DF
more sprite shapes, numbers $E0 to $EF, the player facing each of the four ways
the last sprite shapes, numbers $F0 to $F6: the castle emblem in the panel and the bullet, one shape for each direction it can fly
where the key count waits while the mission screens are up; $404F copies it back into $02AC when the next mission in the same castle begins
where the ammunition waits between two missions of the same castle
where the hit count waits between two missions of the same castle
where the score's top two digits wait between two missions of the same castle
where the score's middle two digits wait between missions
where the score's bottom two digits wait between missions
the mission the player picked on the select screen, 1 to 4 as the game counts them
which floor the mission's prisoner is on, or $FF on the demolition mission, which has none. The room builder compares it with the floor the player is on.
set when the prisoner is in the part of the castle being built, so $4151 puts the prisoner into the room instead of leaving the slot empty

the game's own first code, reached from the mission select. Clears the sixteen icon characters the attract screens borrowed at $2F40, blacks the border and background, clears the mission-in-progress flag and the counters of what the player is carrying, sets the score to six ASCII zeros, and goes to $4946, the top of the game's own loop.

sets a mission going: puts the character set back, clears the game's variables at $02A8 to $02FF, and when a mission has already been played in this castle restores the ammunition, hits, keys and carried items the player ended it with. Then it builds the room ($601B), the panel ($5F9E) and starts the game's interrupt ($4BF2), and waits for the interrupt to report itself running.

sets the eight sprites up for play: no expansion, multicolour for the lower four, the bullet yellow, the screen at $0400 with the play character set at $2000, multicolour text with the two extra backgrounds, and the three sprites of the castle emblem parked in the panel at fixed places. It then puts the player's four sprites round the player's position in $02DF and $02E0: sprites 0 and 2 on the left, 1 and 3 eight pixels further right, 0 and 1 on the top row, 2 and 3 a row of 21 lines below.
blanks the four sprite shapes the player is drawn with, writing zero into both halves of each of the four 64-byte blocks at once through the pointer in $FC

fills all four pages of the screen with the solid black tile $EF and clears colour memory, then points the sprites at their shapes - $C0 to $C3 for the player's four, $F0 to $F2 for the castle emblem in the panel - and colours the panel's two bottom rows

finishes setting the mission up: draws the status panel ($5DC8), clears the message line ($5995), and on the first mission of a castle shows the greeting "WELCOME TO THE EAGLES NEST." from $5694. It then draws the room ($47F1), tells the interrupt to start ($4BF1 = 1), turns all eight sprites on and waits for the interrupt to report back.

the last of the setup: colours the player's four sprites, marks the mission as under way, sets the two shared sprite colours, starts the room's movers ($5ABD) and drops into the game's main loop at $484A
set once a mission has started, so the next mission restores what the player was carrying instead of starting fresh

the player's part of each frame. The low three bits of $02AA say what is going on: 1, 2, 3 or 4 means a room change is in progress and the matching scroll runs a step of it ($432E up, $43D6 down, $4480 left, $4528 right); with none of them set the player takes an ordinary turn at $4297.

the player's turn, once a frame. It works out which tiles are round the player ($5C46), holds everything until fire is let go when $02E3 says a shot is pending, and then counts $02BA up to 3 and acts only on the fourth frame, which is why the player steps one tile every four frames. On that frame it reads control port 2 and goes to the routine for the direction pushed: up $42E2, down $438A, left $4434, right $44DC.

moves the player up a tile when nothing solid is in the way. The four tiles round the player, which $5C46 left in $5C23 to $5C26, must all be below $2D: a tile code of $2D or more is a wall, a door or furniture and stops the move. Otherwise it takes 8 from the player's y, clears the standing-still count, and flips the walking frame. At y = $62 the player is at the top edge of the room, so instead it asks for the room above by setting bits in $02AA.
moves the player down a tile when the four tiles at $5C41 to $5C44 are all below $2D. At y = $B2 the player is at the bottom edge, so it asks for the room below instead by setting bits in $02AA.

moves the picture one row at a time while the player crosses between two rooms up or down, 13 steps counted in $FF. Each step moves the room pointer in $FA on by 128 bytes, takes 8 off the player's y, and brings each shot in the air with it, so a bullet keeps its place in the room rather than on the screen. The last step clears the direction bits in $02AA and leaves only the flag that says a room change is under way.
moves the player left a tile when the four tiles at $5C28, $5C2E and their neighbours are all below $2D, and sets the facing to 3. At the left edge it asks for the room to the left instead.

moves the picture one column at a time while the player crosses into the room on the left, counted down in $FE. Each step moves the room pointer in $FA back a byte, adds 8 to the player's x, and brings each shot in the air with it.

moves the player right a tile when the four tiles at $5C2D, $5C33, $5C39 and $5C3F are all below $2D, and sets the facing to 4. At x = $B0 the player is at the right edge, so it asks for the room to the right instead.

moves the picture one column at a time while the player crosses into the room on the right, counted up in $FE to $64. The mirror of $4480: the room pointer goes on a byte, the player's x comes back 8, and the shots in the air come with it.

fire. It moves the shots already in the air ($4692) and then, if fire is held and this is a fresh press, fires one. The player can have two shots in the air at once: the first is fired when neither is, the second once the first has travelled 8 pixels. With no rounds left it says "OUT OF AMMO!"; otherwise it takes one off the ammunition in decimal mode, redraws the count, points the player's sprites the right way ($46A5), and starts the shot from the player's own position offset by the tables at $4699 and $469D, with five tiles of range.

fires the player's second shot, once the first has travelled at least 8 pixels and no second one is already in the air. It spends a round, points the sprites, and starts the shot at the player with five tiles of range.
how far across the player the shot starts, one byte for each of the four directions
how far down the player the shot starts, one byte for each of the four directions
the first of the player's four sprite shapes for each direction faced: $E0 up, $E4 down, $E8 left, $EC right

points the player's four sprites at the shapes for the way the player is facing, from the table at $46A1, marks a shot as pending, and gives the bullet sprite the shape for that direction, $F3 plus the direction less one
how the bullet sprite is being handled this frame; the interrupt reads it when it places sprite 4
where the bullet sprite sits beside the player for each direction
where the bullet sprite sits below the player for each direction

moves the player's first shot one tile in its direction, if one is in the air. At the edge of the room ($3A at the top, $E2 at the bottom, $20 at the left, $F2 at the right) it flips bit 1 of $02AF instead of going on.
moves the player's second shot one tile in its direction, the same way as $46FA does the first, and counts its distance in $02B4
how many rows of the room are left to draw, counted down from 20

draws the whole room, 28 tiles across and 21 rows down, from the castle map the pointer in $FA names. It is written as a self-modifying loop: the bytes at $4815, $4818 and $481E are the operands of the three instructions in the inner loop, holding the map address, the screen address and the colour address, and the routine rewrites them as it goes. Each tile code goes to the screen and the colour the tile colour table at $8600 gives it goes to colour memory. A row of the map is 128 bytes, so each row adds $80 to the source and 40 to the two destinations.
the operand of the instruction that reads the map: the address of the row being drawn
the operand of the instruction that writes the screen
the operand of the instruction that writes colour memory

hands the machine over to the game: points $0314 at the game's own interrupt at $4AA7, stops CIA 1's timer A, asks for a raster interrupt on line $E9, banks BASIC out and leaves the KERNAL and the I/O in ($01 = $36), and drops into the loop at $4871

the game's main loop, which does nothing itself but watch four things and hand over when one of them happens. $02D3 = $FF means the mission is over ($48F0), $02C8 = 2 that the player is dead ($48D4), $02E9 = 1 that the player has stepped into the lift ($49EC) and 2 that a prisoner has been brought home ($4A5C), and $C5 = $10 that SPACE is down, which pauses. Everything else - the player, the guards, the shots, the panel - is done by the interrupt.

SPACE pauses. It sets the pause flag, waits for SPACE to be let go, and then holds the game: with nothing on the joystick and the message line idle it prints "...PAUSING...", and it keeps printing it until SPACE or the stick is touched, when it clears the flag and the loop goes on.
the player is dead: puts the I/O banking back, pauses the game while the message line empties, turns every sprite off, and goes back to the top of the game at $4946 through $6018
the mission's job is done: pauses the game, clears the message line and waits for it to empty, then goes on to the end-of-mission screens

what happens between missions. Puts the KERNAL's own interrupt back and starts CIA 1's timer A again, so the mission screens have a working keyboard. With no mission in progress it clears the castle flag and asks for a mission ($1D23): mission 1 puts the prisoner in the basement, 2 on the first floor, 3 on the second, and 4, the demolition, has no prisoner, which is $FF in $4010. With a mission already in progress it asks which floor the lift should go to ($1AB2) instead, and keeps the keys, the ammunition, the hits and the three digits of the score in $4009 to $400E while the screens are up.
the player has stepped into the lift: puts the I/O banking back, holds the game while the message line empties, forgets this floor's state and goes back to $4946, which asks which floor to ride to
which of the game's two interrupt bands comes next, flipped between 1 and 0 each time

the game's own interrupt, and where nearly everything in play happens. It serves two bands, flipped by $4AA6: one sets the screen to the play character set at $2000 and does the game's work ($4ACD), then asks for line $E3; the other sets the message line's character set at $2800 with its fine scroll and draws the sprites ($4B4C), then asks for line $FC. It never chains to the KERNAL's handler, so the jiffy clock and the KERNAL's keyboard scan do not run while the game is playing, which is why the game scans SPACE itself.

the interrupt's first band. Puts the screen on the play character set at $2000 in multicolour with 38 columns, keeps the room's movers going ($5AA0), scans SPACE, and then, unless the game is paused or a room change is under way, works through a three-phase rota counted in $02EF: two phases redraw the room ($47F1), the third does the guards, the pickups and the collisions ($4D3A, $5212, $4586, $5A33, $5B1B, $5CB9, $5F27). It ends by stepping the message line's scroll four pixels and shifting the text along when that wraps.
steps the message line four pixels left, and when that has used up a whole character shifts the line's text along ($4BDC) and brings the next character in ($5951)

the interrupt's second band. Puts the screen on the big alphabet at $2800 with the message line's fine scroll in $D016, paints the panel ($600C), draws the room's movers ($5BBA), lets the bullet sprite fade after a hit, runs the player and the room changes ($426F) unless a change is already under way, and places the player's four sprites and the bullet's round the positions in $02DF and $02E0.
how far the game's interrupt has got: the main code sets it to 1 to ask the interrupt to start and waits for 2, then for 3

looks through the tile grid for anything the player has walked onto, skipping the grid's right-hand column. A door key is counted and named, a painting, a vase, cold food, a pendant, first aid and a lift pass are each picked up by their own routine, and a chest found anywhere but the first five places of the grid gives ammunition.
the player walked onto a door key: counts it in decimal mode, says "YOU HAVE FOUND" and "A DOOR KEY.", and clears its two tiles
the player walked onto a painting: says "YOU HAVE FOUND", adds 25 to the score and falls into the shared tail that names it
clears the painting from the map, says "A PAINTING." and redraws the room's tiles
the player walked onto a vase: "YOU HAVE FOUND", 15 points, and the tail that names it
clears the vase from the map, says "A VASE." and redraws
the player walked onto cold food: "YOU HAVE FOUND", and takes $10 off the hits in decimal mode, stopping at none
clears the food from the map, says "SOME COLD FOOD." and redraws
the player walked onto a pendant: "YOU HAVE FOUND" and 40 points
clears the pendant from the map, says "A PENDANT." and redraws
the player walked onto a box of ammunition: adds to the ammunition in decimal mode and stops at $99, and when there is no room for any more says "ANY MORE AMMO WOULD BE WASTED !"
the player walked onto first aid: "YOU HAVE FOUND", and clears the hits altogether
works back from the place in the tile grid to the map address of the object's own corner, clears its five tiles, scores it, redraws the room and says "FIRST AID."
the player walked onto a lift pass: "YOU HAVE FOUND", clears it from the grid, says "A LIFT PASS." and marks the pass as carried
rubs an object out of the tile grid, which the redraw then takes to the screen

works out where in the castle map a place on the screen is. The room's top left corner is x = $20, y = $3A, a tile is eight pixels square and a row of the map is 128 bytes, so the address is the room pointer in $FA plus 16 times the pixels down plus an eighth of the pixels across. It leaves the address in $02 and $03.

looks up the map tile each shot in the air has reached. Tiles $3E and $3F and the codes below $08 are air, so the shot flies on; anything else stops it. On a hit the shot is taken out of the air, its direction is kept in $02D2 and $529B decides what was hit.

decides what a shot hit, by the tile code. $76 to $C0 and $D4 to $E3 are the soldiers and officers, $30 to $3E and $C0 to $CB and $E7 to $EE are walls that just stop it, $5E to $6D a soldier that falls, $49 and $4A the two halves of a steel door, $47 and $48 a wooden door, $43 to $46 a mirror that shortens the shot's range to three, $40 to $FB the furniture, and anything else is looked for in the six-by-six grid around the shot, where the nine places listed at $5374 are checked for the code of a pickup.
the nine places in the six-by-six tile grid a shot looks at to find what it hit, since an object is drawn from several tiles and only its first one names it
a shot has set a detonator off: marks this floor's charge as armed in $5F9A plus the floor, says "DETONATOR ACTIVATED.", and scores it
the shot hit something that is no use: says "YOU ARE WAISTING AMMO." (the game's own spelling) and leaves the shot's range at two
a shot hit an open chest, which breaks what is in it: clears the two tiles of the chest and scores it
the shot hit a painting, which is picked up all the same: says "YOU HAVE SHOT", and $4ECD names it and clears it
the shot hit cold food; $4F27 names it and clears it
the shot hit a pendant; $4F51 names it and clears it
the shot hit a vase; $4EF7 names it and clears it
the shot hit first aid; $4FA5 names it and clears it
the shot hit one of the four pieces of furniture, codes $4C to $4F, and turns it into the broken shape $50 to $53, two tiles on the top row and two on the row below
the shot hit a lift pass, which is no use at all: "SHOOTING A LIFT PASS IS A BIT SILLY !"
a shot hit the right half of a steel door, code $49: sets the door's state and opens it from $50F7
a shot hit the left half of a steel door, code $4A, and opens it the same way
a shot hit the lower half of a wooden door, code $47, which can be shot open: $5192 does it
a shot hit the upper half of a wooden door, code $48; the same as $54F3 with the map address moved up a row

a shot hit a soldier or an officer, codes $5E to $6D. The twelve codes are the three shapes each of four kinds, and each kind takes the shot in its own place: the tile hit is moved left, right, up or down to find the figure's own square before it is knocked down.
the game's 33 messages for the line at the bottom of the screen, ASCII, each ending "@" ($40); facts.md lists them
prints a message on the line at the bottom of the screen. $FC and $FD point at the text, which is ASCII ending "@".

writes every number on the status panel: the keys at row 4, the ammunition at row 6, the hits at row 8 and the six digits of the score at row 11, each as two screen codes from $5A20. On the way it also works out where the player is in the castle, in tiles, and leaves it in $02CA and $02CB.

turns one binary-coded-decimal byte into the two screen codes that print it. The play character set keeps its digits at $F0 to $F9, so each nibble only has to be ORed with $F0; the upper one is shifted down first. Every number on the panel goes through here.
the six-by-six block of map tiles around the player or another mover, read by $5C55. The movement tests read the four of them the player's own square covers.
the four tile codes the player's own square overlaps, worked out each frame by $5C46; every one must be below $2D for a move to be allowed
works out which tiles surround the player, from the position in $02DF and $02E0, by way of $51CD and $5C55, and leaves them in the grid at $5C22

reads the six-by-six block of map tiles around the place the pointer in $06 names into the grid at $5C22, six bytes a row. A row of the map is 128 bytes away, which the routine reaches by setting bit 7 of Y and stepping the pointer's high byte, so it never needs a second pointer.
one byte a floor, set to 1 once that floor's charge has been armed; the castle blows up when all four are

the game's own one-key scan: it drives keyboard row 7 and reads column 4, which is SPACE, and leaves $10 in $C5 while the key is down and 0 when it is up. The game keeps its own flag in the byte the KERNAL uses for the key it last saw, and nothing else on the keyboard is read.
the four tiles the prisoner is drawn from when facing up
the four tiles the prisoner is drawn from when facing down
the four tiles the prisoner is drawn from when facing left
the four tiles the prisoner is drawn from when facing right
the sound chip's and the player's own housekeeping, from $6009 and $600C: it takes a hit when one is due, silences and sets the chip up ($63B7), and runs the sound effects a frame at a time ($63E6)

silences all 25 sound registers by writing 8 and then 0 to each, sets the volume to 15 with the low-pass filter on, the cutoff to $50 and the resonance to 2, and builds the table of random numbers at $67CA
the sound, once a frame. It plays a footstep when the player has stepped, starts the effect $02D5 asks for, or carries on the one already playing.
starts one of the nine effects on voice 1, each with its own attack and decay, pulse width, frequency and waveform, and its own length in $02D7
effect 1, for a shot going home: a short pulse note at $01C8 with a fast attack and no sustain
effect 2, for a shot that hits something that does not matter
carries the sound in progress on, a frame at a time: most of the nine count $02D7 down and then let the note go by clearing the waveform, and some change the waveform part way through
counts the effect's frames down and silences voice 1 when they run out
the same tail for another of the effects
an effect that changes its waveform to a triangle with 16 frames left before it stops
the player's footsteps, on voice 2: a short note at $0A00 or $0500 depending on which foot it is, taken from the walking frame

fills 256 bytes at $8700 with random numbers. It sets voice 3 to noise at the highest frequency and reads the oscillator's own output at $D41B 256 times, which is the SID's noise generator used as the game's dice, then silences the voice again. Called once, from the sound set-up.
steps the index on and returns the next byte of the random table in A

builds the castle's map for a floor out of the floor's own description. Every byte of the description names a block of four tiles by four, kept at $7000 plus sixteen times the byte, and the routine copies the block's sixteen bytes into the map, four to a row and 128 bytes between rows. Certain bytes mean more than a block as well: $30 to $37 are the four kinds of figure, each of which is added to the list of figures in $8100 to $8500, $62 is the lift, whose place is kept in $02EA, and $63 is the prisoner, whose place is kept in $02ED. It is why a whole floor of the castle takes only a few hundred bytes to describe.

builds a whole floor of the castle. It banks every ROM out so the RAM beneath them can be reached ($01 = $30), takes the floor's description from $D000 plus a kilobyte for each floor, and works through it as 32 rows of 32 bytes, each byte a block of four tiles by four. The map it builds starts at $9000 and is 128 tiles across, so a floor fills 16 kilobytes from a kilobyte of description. Every figure, the lift and the prisoner are picked out of the description as it goes.
"THE PRISONER IS VERY CLOSE.", the only message kept away from the block at $5609
the blocks the castle's floors are built from, sixteen bytes each: four tiles across and four down. A byte of a floor's description names one, and its address is $7000 plus sixteen times the byte.
more of the blocks the floors are built from
where each figure on this floor is, across the floor in blocks; one byte a figure
where each figure on this floor is, down the floor in blocks; one byte a figure
the low byte of each figure's place in the castle map
the high byte of each figure's place in the castle map
what each figure is, 1 to 4: the kinds the description's bytes $34 and $35, $30 and $31, $36 and $37, and $32 and $33 stand for

the colour of each tile of the play screen's character set, one byte a tile. The attract screens read it for the icons they show ($8600, $8614, $8618 to $861B, $8628 and $8666), and the castle's rooms are coloured from it.
256 random bytes, built at start-up from the sound chip's noise oscillator and read a byte at a time by $67F3

999 bytes of tile-shaped graphics, 125 characters' worth, that the tape loads and no instruction in the game reaches, by name or through a pointer built from an immediate. What they are is open; they are shaped like a second set of wall and floor tiles.

the floor the player is on, built from its description into 128 tiles across by 128 down, one byte a tile. It is 16 kilobytes, which is why it lies over the title picture at $A000 and the RAM under the I/O area is used for the descriptions.
the basement's description, a kilobyte: 32 rows of 32 bytes, each naming one of the blocks at $7000
the ground floor's description, in the same form
the first floor's description, in the same form
the second floor's description, in the same form

the multicolour bitmap of the stone plaque reading "Into The Eagle's Nest...", which the credits, supplies and valuables screens show across the top of the screen. The video chip reads it from bank 3 while the first band of the interrupt is in force.
the middle of the plaque's bitmap
the bottom of the plaque's bitmap
the colour memory the plaque's bitmap is drawn with, which in bitmap mode is the screen at $EC00. The name-entry screen copies $EE00 and $EF00 of it into the real colour memory.
the KERNAL's own table of interrupt vectors, showing through in the RAM beneath the ROM. No instruction in the game names it.
